# ============================================================================
# ERN landing page for the 2024 Cityscape paper (Thomas, Ramiller, Ren, and
# Toomet). Edit the copy here, then rebuild:
#
#     quarto render cityscape-2024.qmd
#
# That overwrites cityscape-2024.html in place. Review
# `git diff cityscape-2024.html` before committing.
#
# The page chrome lives in _extensions/ern/paper/template.html and the
# page-only styles in assets/css/paper-2026.css. Every heading, paragraph,
# table cell, link, and footer entry is a field below.
#
# Values are parsed as Markdown. Do not backslash-escape inside a folded
# block scalar (>-); YAML keeps the backslash and it lands on the page.
#
# FACT DISCIPLINE. Every number, quotation, and claim about the paper was
# checked against the PDF on the site
# (assets/papers/thomas_ramiller_ren_toomet_2024_cityscape_26-1.pdf; page
# numbers are the journal's running footers, pp. 241-259). Exhibit A.1
# (p. 254) is the source of the table. The two 2021 law dates were checked
# on app.leg.wa.gov on 2026-11-10: RCW 59.18.650 (2021 c 212, just cause)
# and RCW 59.18.640 (2021 c 115, appointed counsel). Do not add a figure
# without doing the same.
#
# CONFIRMED BY TIM, 2026-11-10 (not in the paper): the legislative
# testimony and coalition work in policy.paras[1]; "one of the first states"
# for appointed counsel; the peer-reviewed kicker; Alex Ramiller is now at
# the University of Toronto. ESSB 5600's text (bill as passed, sec. 1-3) was
# read on lawfilesext.leg.wa.gov the same day for policy.laws[0]. The paper
# does not name right to counsel; the page says so.
#
# Converted from hand-written legacy HTML (Bootstrap, main.css, v5b.css) to
# the 2026 design system on 2026-11-10.
# ============================================================================

    A UC Berkeley and University of Washington team used natural language
    processing to read 111,740 eviction court records in four Washington
    counties and estimate racial and gender disparities in filings. Published
    in Cityscape (HUD, 2024).
  short_description: >-
    How the Eviction Research Network used natural language processing to
    read 111,740 Washington eviction court records and estimate racial and
    gender disparities in filings.
  og_title: "Toward a National Eviction Data Collection Strategy Using NLP (Cityscape 2024)"
  keywords: >-
    eviction data, natural language processing, NLP, court records, Washington
    State evictions, Cityscape, HUD, racial disparity, gender disparity,
    Bayesian race estimation, demographic estimation, Tim Thomas, Eviction
    Research Network, UC Berkeley
  author: "Eviction Research Network, UC Berkeley"
  canonical: "https://evictionresearch.net/cityscape-2024.html"

  eyebrow: "Peer-reviewed article · Cityscape 26(1) · HUD PD&amp;R"
  h1_lead: "Toward a National Eviction Data Collection Strategy"
  h1_em: "Using Natural Language Processing"
  lede: >-
    How the Eviction Research Network read 111,740 Washington eviction court
    records from scanned PDF and TIFF images, and estimated racial and gender
    disparities that county-level counts do not show.
  meta: >-
    **Tim Thomas** and **Alex Ramiller**, UC Berkeley · **Cheng Ren**,
    University at Albany, SUNY · **Ott Toomet**, University of

# All four match the paper: 111,740 images (p. 246), the four counties,
# 2004-2017 (p. 246), 93% rooftop-to-block (p. 248).
stats:
  - v: "111,740"
    l: "court record images processed"
  - v: "4"
    l: "Washington counties"
  - v: "2004–2017"
    l: "years of filings"
  - v: "93%"
    l: "of addresses geocoded to rooftop-to-block accuracy"

intro:
  eyebrow: "About the paper"
  h2_lead: "Why court records"
  h2_em: "need a pipeline"
  paras:
    - >-
      Many states have no formal process to digitize, count, or release
      eviction filings, and some publish only county-level counts. In those
      states the names and addresses that show who is evicted, and from which
      neighborhoods, sit in scanned court images or paper files.
    - >-
      The 2024 *Cityscape* paper lays out the pipeline the Eviction Research
      Network built for Washington State and proposes a strategy for
      collecting eviction data across the country. The team downloaded
      111,740 court record images from Pierce, Snohomish, Whatcom, and King
      counties, converted them to text with optical character recognition
      (OCR), and extracted defendant addresses with rule-based matching and a
      spaCy named-entity recognizer. It then geocoded the addresses and
      estimated race and gender with published R packages, checking the
      estimates against legal-aid intake data.
    - >-
      In Pierce County, **one in five** Black female-headed renter households
      was named in an eviction filing between 2013 and 2017. In King County,
      it was one in nine. The state's own records counted filings only by
      county.
  glance:
    heading: "The paper's sections"
    items:
      - name: "Background."
        body: "The eviction process, the records it creates, and the current state of national eviction data collection."
      - name: "Data and methods."
        body: "Court record access, OCR, address extraction, geocoding, validation, and race and gender estimation."
      - name: "Findings."
        body: "Household eviction rates by race and gender, judgment amounts, and neighborhood patterns in four counties."
      - name: "Future strategies."
        body: "Document layout analysis and large language models."
      - name: "Conclusion."
        body: "A recommended strategy for collecting eviction data nationally."

contributions:
  eyebrow: "Contributions"
  h2_lead: "What the paper"
  h2_em: "contributes"
  points:
    - title: "OCR and text extraction can read scanned court records at scale"
      body: >-
        Tesseract OCR converted 111,740 PDF and TIFF images to text, and
        rule-based matching plus spaCy named-entity recognition extracted
        defendant addresses. A Naive Bayes model put 98% confidence on the
        correct address.
    # Geocoder list and results: p. 247-248. Google is not among the five
    # tested (the legacy page said it was).
    - title: "Geocoders differ in coverage and in replicability"
      body: >-
        The team tested OpenStreetMap, the Census Bureau geocoder, King
        County's address file, Esri Business Analyst, and Azure on about 5,000
        hand-extracted 2013 King County addresses. Azure geocoded the most.
        Among tools whose results can be reproduced later, Esri Business
        Analyst did best.
    - title: "Surname-based race estimates came within several percentage points of intake data"
      body: >-
        Imai and Khanna's `wru` package, backed by Xie's `rethnicity` Bi-LSTM
        model, produced race estimates within several percentage points of
        King County legal-aid intake data. The training data were voter files
        from Southern states, so estimates outside the South need extra
        caution.
    # Exhibit A.1: Black female is the highest rate in each county.
    - title: "Black female-headed households had the highest filing rates in every county"
      body: >-
        The rates were 11% against 6% to 7% for White-headed households in
        King, 19% against 13% to 16% in Pierce, and 12% against 8% to 10% in
        Snohomish. Whatcom's 26% rests on 15 cases.
    - title: "Court access depended on each clerk"
      body: >-
        One clerk granted access readily and two others through local legal
        aid. A fourth would not waive a 25-cent page fee, an estimated
        $350,000 for 2004 to 2017. The technical pipeline is portable, but
        access may take a legislative mandate, grant support, or a legal-aid
        partner.
    - title: "Layout analysis and language models could lower the barrier"
      body: >-
        The paper tested large language models such as ChatGPT on the 2013
        court records and flags privacy risks and accuracy gaps. It also
        points to document layout analysis, which combines computer vision and
        NLP. Both could let researchers with less programming experience do
        this work.

pipeline:
  eyebrow: "The pipeline"
  h2_lead: "From court image to"
  h2_em: "demographic estimate"
  sub: >-
    The paper documents each of the five stages so that other teams can
    reproduce the pipeline or adapt it to their own courts' records.
  groups:
    - label: "Case study area"
      pills: ["King County", "Pierce County", "Snohomish County", "Whatcom County"]
    - label: "Tools"
      pills: ["Tesseract OCR", "spaCy NER", "Azure Maps", "Esri Business Analyst", "wru (R)", "rethnicity (R)", "gender (R)"]
  steps:
    - name: "Access and download"
      body: >-
        With case numbers from a state records request made with the
        Washington Office of Civil Legal Aid, a scraper pulled 111,740
        eviction case images from Washington's court portals, pausing between
        requests so as not to overload the servers.
    - name: "OCR and text cleaning"
      body: >-
        Tesseract OCR converted scanned PDF and TIFF summonses into text.
        Common errors, such as a "1" read as "|", a superscript "th" read as a
        quote mark, and row numbers caught inside addresses, were handled in
        post-processing.
    - name: "Address extraction"
      body: >-
        Rule-based regular expressions (house numbers, street types, and ZIP
        Code patterns) ran first, then spaCy named-entity recognition. A
        Naive Bayes model scored each candidate address; the correct defendant
        address had 98% confidence. Against 2013 addresses extracted by hand,
        the method was 93% accurate. The usual error was picking up the
        court's or the attorney's address.
    - name: "Geocoding and validation"
      body: >-
        Addresses that resolved only to a street or county centroid were
        dropped, leaving 93% at rooftop-to-block accuracy. Against
        hand-extracted 2013 addresses, the extracted addresses had an average
        Levenshtein ratio of 0.82.
    - name: "Race and gender estimation"
      body: >-
        The R package `wru` (Imai and Khanna) estimated race by Bayesian
        inference from surname and tract composition, and `rethnicity` (Xie)
        handled the remaining names with a Bi-LSTM model. The `gender` package
        (Mullen et al.) inferred gender from first names checked against SSA
        and IPUMS records. Estimates agreed with King County Bar Housing
        Justice Project intake data within several percentage points.

findings:
  eyebrow: "Washington findings"
  h2_lead: "Eviction filing rates by"
  h2_em: "race and gender"
  paras:
    - >-
      Black female-headed renter households had the highest five-year filing
      rate in every county, from 11% in King to 19% in Pierce. Pierce County's
      rates ran high for every group, from 12% to 19%. The paper describes
      Pierce as one of the largest destinations for movers from King County
      and the rest of the country.
  table:
    row_heading: "Householder group"
    columns: ["King", "Pierce", "Snohomish", "Whatcom"]
    caption: "Five-year eviction rates by race and gender of householder, King, Pierce, Snohomish, and Whatcom counties, 2013–2017"
    source: >-
      Source: Thomas, Ramiller, Ren, and Toomet (2024), Exhibit A.1.
      Denominators are estimated renter households from ACS 5-year estimates;
      numerators are estimated heads of household named in unlawful detainer
      filings, identified through the NLP pipeline. Darker cells mark higher
      rates.
    # v is the rate in percent, Exhibit A.1 (p. 254); all 40 cells checked
    # 2026-11-05. mark adds a footnote sign after the value.
    rows:
      - group: "Black female"
        cells: [{v: 11}, {v: 19}, {v: 12}, {v: 26, mark: "&#42;"}]
      - group: "Black male"
        cells: [{v: 8}, {v: 15}, {v: 7}, {v: 6}]
      - group: "Asian female"
        cells: [{v: 6}, {v: 16}, {v: 10}, {v: 5}]
      - group: "Asian male"
        cells: [{v: 4}, {v: 16}, {v: 9}, {v: 6}]
      - group: "Latinx female"
        cells: [{v: 8}, {v: 14}, {v: 8}, {v: 5}]
      - group: "Latinx male"
        cells: [{v: 8}, {v: 12}, {v: 10}, {v: 4}]
      - group: "White female"
        cells: [{v: 6}, {v: 13}, {v: 8}, {v: 5}]
      - group: "White male"
        cells: [{v: 7}, {v: 16}, {v: 10}, {v: 7}]
      - group: "Other race/ethnicity female"
        cells: [{v: 5}, {v: 12}, {v: 7}, {v: 3}]
      - group: "Other race/ethnicity male"
        cells: [{v: 8}, {v: 13}, {v: 10}, {v: 5}]
  note: >-
    &#42; Hatched: the Whatcom County Black female rate rests on 15 named
    defendants.
    The Pierce County rate, the paper's headline figure, rests on 1,392
    filings against an estimated 7,233 Black female-headed renter households.

summary:
  eyebrow: "Summary"
  h2_lead: "The paper"
  h2_em: "in depth"
  paras:
    # p. 244: neither effort can capture records that appear only in
    # unstructured formats.
    - >-
      The two national eviction data efforts, Eviction Lab and the Legal
      Services Corporation (LSC), collect structured records and cannot
      capture filings that exist only as scanned images or paper files, the
      paper finds. Eviction Lab receives datasets from collaborators or buys
      them from vendors; LSC scrapes digital data from county court systems.
    - >-
      Washington's legislature asked for estimates of racial and gender
      disparities in eviction, and the state's own counts existed only at the
      county level. The records sit on three web portals, and each elected
      county clerk decides who gets access. One clerk would not waive a charge
      of 25 cents per downloaded page, an estimated $350,000 for the records
      from 2004 to 2017.
  # Verbatim, p. 253, first lines of "Conclusion and Discussion".
  quote:
    text: >-
      "Combining data science tools with existing eviction data collection
      efforts can fill in massive gaps. The NLP approach can extract addresses
      from court record images, creating the opportunity to analyze
      demographic disparities in the State of Washington and create a clearer
      picture of who was being evicted and from where."
    cite: "Thomas, Ramiller, Ren, and Toomet (2024), p. 253"
  sections:
    # p. 252, end of Findings.
    - heading: "Where eviction rates peaked"
      paras:
        - >-
          Eviction rates peaked in the region's lowest-rent and most racially
          diverse neighborhoods. In King County, cases were more frequent
          in South Seattle's diverse neighborhoods in the earlier years and
          then grew outside the city in South King County, both known
          displacement destinations for Black, Indigenous, Latinx, and Asian
          households. In Pierce and Snohomish counties, evictions concentrated
          in segregated urban areas.
    # pp. 253-254.
    - heading: "What this means for other jurisdictions"
      paras:
        - >-
          The case study is Washington, but the method is general. OCR,
          address extraction, geocoding, validation, and demographic
          estimation each use tools the paper names (pp. 253–254), and teams
          in states without complete Eviction Lab or LSC coverage can start
          from them.
        - >-
          The paper also sets two conditions for scaling the approach. An
          interdisciplinary team has to guard privacy and data integrity at
          every step, and court officers may cooperate only with a legislative
          mandate or grant support.

policy:
  eyebrow: "Policy context"
  h2_lead: "Washington"
  h2_em: "tenant protections"
  paras:
    # pp. 241-242 ("helped pass", "motivated the adoption") and p. 253.
    - >-
      The paper reports that this research helped pass several statewide
      tenant protections, including the 2019 extension of the pay-or-vacate
      notice from 3 to 14 days (ESSB 5600) and just-cause eviction
      protections.
    # Not in the paper; confirmed by Tim 2026-11-10.
    - >-
      The estimates produced by the pipeline were used in legislative
      testimony and in coalition work with the Washington Office of Civil
      Legal Aid, the King County Bar Housing Justice Project, and tenant
      attorneys across the four counties in the study. None of these reforms
      is attributable to a single study.
  laws:
    - year: "2019"
      name: "Pay-or-vacate notice extended from 3 to 14 days"
      cite: "ESSB 5600 (2019 c 356) · named in the paper"
      body: "Replaced the 3-day notice to pay rent or vacate with a 14-day notice in a set form. The same law created a state payment to landlords in some eviction cases, to give tenants more time to find the resources to stay."
    - year: "2021"
      name: "Statewide just cause"
      cite: "RCW 59.18.650 (2021 c 212) · named in the paper"
      body: "A landlord may end a tenancy only for a cause the statute lists, with limited exceptions for fixed-term leases."
    - year: "2021"
      name: "Appointed counsel for low-income tenants"
      cite: "RCW 59.18.640 (2021 c 115) · not named in the paper"
      body: "Courts must appoint an attorney for indigent tenants in unlawful detainer cases, subject to funding. Washington was one of the first states to guarantee it."

  h2_em: "team"

    including the Snohomish, Pierce, and Whatcom Counties court clerks and
